tagline.text: A harvest-festival town where the whole village blooms with rice-wafer decorations

location.label: Location
location.text: Lucban, Quezon (at the foot of Mount Banahaw)

items.credit: Ralff Nestor Nacor / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A cool mountain town at the foot of Mount Banahaw, famous for the Pahiyas Festival every May 15, when every household decorates its walls with colorful rice-wafer ornaments called kiping and farm produce. With an 18th-century Baroque church, the hilltop pilgrimage site Kamay ni Hesus, and local specialties like pancit habhab and longganisa, it's a food-lover's getaway too.
Lucban is a small town in southwestern Quezon province, at the foot of Mount Banahaw, a mountain Filipinos regard as sacred. It's about
southeast of Manila and about
22km

from Lucena, the capital of Quezon province. Being upland at the mountain's base, the air is cooler and rain more frequent than in the lowlands, earning it the nickname "the summer capital of Quezon"; the town's name is said to come from the pomelo tree once common here, called "lukban."
After Franciscan friars founded a mission town in
, Lucban prospered from the Spanish era onward on fertile rice paddies and coconut farming. The town-center church, San Luis Obispo de Tolosa, burned down in a
fire and was rebuilt into its present Baroque form by
, its moss-covered stone facade and octagonal bell tower showing nearly three centuries of age.
What put Lucban on the national map is the Pahiyas Festival, honoring San Isidro Labrador, patron saint of farmers. Every
May 15

, houses along the procession route cover their walls and roofs with kiping — colorful decorations made by pressing rice-flour batter into leaf-shaped molds and drying it — along with rice stalks, vegetables, fruit, and longganisa, giving thanks for the year's harvest. There's also a contest for the most beautiful house, and today, with giant puppet parades and street performances added in, it has grown into a week-long celebration.

Even outside festival season, Lucban is plenty appealing as a quiet small-town destination — walking the church grounds and old lanes, tasting local dishes like pancit habhab and longganisa, and climbing to the hilltop pilgrimage site. It's a good pick for travelers who want a close look at rural Philippine faith and food culture, and for anyone hoping to photograph the festival.
Around
May 15

, houses along the procession route are decked out in kiping and farm produce. The route changes each year, so start at the church and stroll slowly through the decorated lanes, taking in each house's distinct display.

Kiping is made by spreading rice-flour batter thinly on a leaf, drying it, and dyeing it in bright colors; grilled or fried, it can also be eaten like a cracker. After the festival, there's a custom of taking the decorations down and sharing them to eat.
An 18th-century church with a three-tier Baroque facade and an octagonal bell tower. It holds a relic of the town's patron saint, and the Pahiyas Festival's dawn Mass also begins here.

A pilgrimage site on a hill on the edge of town — climb around 300 steps past Stations of the Cross statues to reach a giant statue of Christ with arms outstretched, overlooking all of Lucban. There's also a church known for a model of Noah's Ark and healing Masses.

Lucban's signature noodle dish, served on a banana leaf and slurped straight from it without utensils. Splashing on a little vinegar is the local way to eat it, and it's easy to find at the market and on the street.

A small sausage with strong garlic and oregano notes, salty and tangy, widely regarded as one of the Philippines' top regional longganisas. Vacuum-packed ones from the market make good gifts to bring home.

blocks.title: Tayabas Basilica and the old bridge

children.text: About
20–30 minutes
by car to neighboring Tayabas, where you can see the Minor Basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel, famous for its key-shaped floor plan, along with a Spanish-era stone bridge.
Depart Manila (private car, or a bus to Lucena)
Arrive in Lucban, breakfast of longganisa and rice near the market
Walk Lucban Church, its plaza, and the old lanes
Tricycle to Kamay ni Hesus, climb the steps for the view by the Christ statue
Lunch of pancit habhab and jardinera
Head to Tayabas to see Tayabas Basilica
Shop for gifts like longganisa and broas at Lucban market
Depart for Manila
Arrive in Lucban, check in, watch households putting the finishing touches on their decorations
Walk the lit-up festival streets and the church at night
Attend the dawn Mass at the church, or take photos on the streets before the crowds arrive
Walk the procession route admiring decorated houses, taste pancit habhab and kiping
Watch the San Isidro procession and giant puppet parade, then head home

On festival day, entry into town is controlled and the crowds are enormous. The schedule shifts slightly year to year, so check the latest notices from the Lucban tourism office, and book lodging months in advance.
Direct buses to Lucban are rare. From Manila's Buendia, PITX, Cubao, and other terminals, take a Lucena-bound bus run by JAC Liner, DLTB, JAM, and others to Lucena Grand Terminal, about
3–4 hours
, for a fare of about
one way.
From Lucena Grand Terminal or downtown, a Lucban-bound jeepney passes through Tayabas to reach Lucban's public market. It takes about
45 minutes–1 hour
, for a fare of about
. There are also jeepney routes coming over from Santa Cruz and Pagsanjan in Laguna province via Magdalena and Majayjay.

There are two routes: take SLEX, switch to Maharlika Highway at Santo Tomas, and pass through Tiaong and Candelaria to Tayabas; or take the Laguna mountain route through Calamba, Los Baños, Pagsanjan, and Majayjay. Either way takes about
3–4 hours
, and the Laguna route is good for stopping at waterfalls and old churches along the way.
The town center is walkable, and it's about
10 minutes
to Kamay ni Hesus by tricycle, for about
per vehicle. During the festival, vehicle traffic is blocked, so you'll mostly need to walk.
Since Lucban sits at the foot of Mount Banahaw, rain falls fairly evenly through the year and the dry season is short and not sharply defined. The relatively dry, clear stretch is
March–May
, with daytime temperatures around
, a bit cooler than Manila. Around
May 15
, when the Pahiyas Festival takes place, the town is at its most spectacular but also its most crowded.
June–October
sees frequent rain from the southwest monsoon and typhoons, and
November–February

brings cloudy, rainy days to eastern Quezon from the northeast monsoon, though mornings and evenings are cool and good for walking. It's worth carrying an umbrella regardless of season. Note that Kamay ni Hesus draws large crowds of pilgrims during Holy Week.
Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Downtown Lucban has plenty of small inns and homestays (transient houses), and the outskirts have farm-style resorts with gardens and pools. Ordinarily it runs about

per night, but rates climb sharply during the Pahiyas Festival and rooms book out months ahead. If you can't find a room for the festival, staying in Lucena or Tayabas and coming in early morning is another option.

In Lucban, the food is half the trip. Signature dishes include pancit habhab, eaten by hand off a banana leaf; garlicky Lucban longganisa; jardinera, a festive dish of egg, meat, and pineapple steamed in a mold; and broas, a crisp sponge cookie. "Buddy's," open since
, is Lucban's signature restaurant for trying all this local food in one place. About
per meal is plenty, and pancit habhab is much cheaper still at market stalls.
Take your Pahiyas Festival photos early in the morning, before the crowds arrive. Decorations are usually finished the evening before the festival, so it's worth walking around the night before too.
On festival day, roads into town back up for hours. Parking on the outskirts and walking in is actually faster than driving.
The decorated houses are people's homes. Don't touch or remove decorations without asking, and if you want to go inside, ask permission first.
Eating pancit habhab without utensils is traditional, but if that's tricky, it's fine to ask the vendor for a fork. Bring wet wipes.
Longganisa spoils quickly at room temperature, so pack it in a cooler or insulated bag.
The steps up to Kamay ni Hesus have little shade. Bring a hat and water, and climb during the cooler morning or late afternoon.
This is a rain-prone area, so bring a folding umbrella and quick-drying shoes.
If you're taking the Laguna route, it's easy to build a full day around Pagsanjan Falls, Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, and a Majayjay church stop.

During the Pahiyas Festival, tens of thousands of people crowd the narrow lanes, so pickpocketing and lost children are common. Wear valuables in front, and agree on a meeting point with kids and your group beforehand. Check the latest notices from Lucban town for traffic controls and the event schedule.
To protect the environment, Mount Banahaw's trails have long been closed or open only on a limited basis. Don't enter the mountain without a permit, and follow notices from the managing agency.
Inside the church, refrain from taking photos during Mass, and avoid revealing clothing.
After rain, the steps at Kamay ni Hesus and the stone pavement of the old lanes get slippery.
Hygiene varies among the food stalls on the festival streets. Choose ones that are busy and cooking food fresh.
When a typhoon passes through, the mountain roads connecting to Lucena can see landslides or flooding.
About
1 hour
by car via the Laguna mountain road, Laguna's signature attraction, reached by paddling a boat up the gorge to the base of the falls.
About
1 hour
by car, a national historic site with an underground crypt beneath a Spanish-era church cemetery.
About
1 hour–1 hour 30 minutes
by car, a coconut plantation resort where you dine with your feet in the water at a restaurant beneath a waterfall.
About
1 hour
by car to Mauban port, a quiet island reached by boat, with vast sandy flats exposed at low tide.
About
2 hours
by car, an island off Padre Burgos with striking rock formations and white sand, one of Quezon's beach spots.
